intro: Money is everywhere. You see it at the store. You see prices on signs. Grown-ups earn money at work. In this unit you will learn what money is for.
You will learn coins and what they are worth. You will pay and count change. You will make a plan to save, spend and share your money.
At the end, you can make a plan for your own money. You can wait for something big. You can help others too. You will know how money works.
bigQuestion: What is money for, and how can I use it well?

timeline.t: People trade things, like a cookie for an apple
Trading gets stuck when people want different things
People agree to use money to trade
We learn coins: penny, nickel, dime, quarter
We read prices and pay, then count our change
We earn money by doing work
We save, spend and share with three jars
We keep money safe in a bank

words.d: to give something and get something back, when both people agree
trading things for other things, without money
coins and bills that people agree to take when they buy and sell
how much money something costs
money you get back when you pay more than the price
to get money for doing work
to keep money now so you can use it later
a business that keeps people's money safe

choices: Giving something and getting something back
test.why: In a trade, both people swap.

test.q: Why is money easier than barter?
test.why: People agree to take money, so trading is easy.

test.q: How many cents is a nickel?
Which coin is worth the most?
test.why: A quarter is 25 cents, the most here.

test.q: A toy costs 60 cents (an example). You pay $1. What is your change?
How do most people get money?
test.why: Most people earn money at work.

test.q: A ball costs $3 (an example). You save $1 a week. How many weeks?
What are the three jars for?
test.why: The three jars split money three ways.
A bank keeps your money safe.

test.q: You have $1. You buy a sticker for $1. What do you give up?
test.why: One dollar can be spent or saved, not both.

write.prompt: You earn $3 a week (an example). You want a $6 kite (an example). Make a plan. How much will you save, spend and share each week? How many weeks until the kite?
tips: Say how much goes in each jar.
Say what you give up to wait.
Tell why your plan is a good one.

title: Money, Saving and Spending

chapters.title: What Money Is For
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people use money instead of just trading things?

story.title: The Lunch Table Trade
story.kicker: Two friends try to trade, and the class finds a better way.
paragraphs: Maya had two cookies. She wanted an apple. Leo had an apple. Maya said, "Trade you a cookie for your apple." Leo shook his head. He did not want a cookie. He wanted a pencil.
Maya did not have a pencil. Sam had a pencil. But Sam wanted a sticker, not a cookie. Now three kids were stuck. Nobody could get what they wanted. The trade went wrong.
Their teacher had an idea. She gave each child paper tickets. "Everyone takes tickets," she said. "Pay with tickets. Then use the tickets to buy what you want."
Maya paid Leo tickets for the apple. Leo paid Sam tickets for a pencil. Sam bought a sticker. Everyone got what they wanted. The tickets worked like money.
story.think: Why did the tickets make trading easier than cookies?

lessons.title: A Trade Needs Two Yeses
lessons.mainIdea: A trade happens when both people agree to swap.
reading: A *trade* is a swap. You give something. You get something back. Both people must say yes.
Ana has a red crayon. Ben has a blue crayon. Ana wants blue. Ben wants red. They both say yes. The trade works!
If Ben says no, there is no trade. Nobody can make you trade. Both sides must agree.

words.d: to give something and get something back, when both people agree

look.title: Two Friends, Two Toys
look.text: Look at two friends on the rug. Lily holds a toy car. Omar holds a toy truck. Lily wants the truck. Omar wants the car.

check.q: What does a trade need?
check.why: A trade needs both people to agree.

check.q: Ana gives a red crayon and gets a blue one. What is this?
check.why: She gave something and got something back. That is a trade.

check.q: Ben does not want Ana's crayon. What happens?
check.why: Both must say yes. Ben said no, so there is no trade.

lessons.title: When Trading Gets Stuck
lessons.mainIdea: Trading is hard when the other person does not want what you have.
reading: Trading is hard sometimes. You must find someone with what you want. They must also want what you have.
Kim has a banana. She wants a book. Jay has a book. Jay wants a ball, not a banana. Kim is stuck. She cannot trade.
Long ago, people traded things like food and cloth. They had this same problem. It took lots of time.

words.d: trading things for other things, without money

look.title: The Stuck Trade
look.text: Picture Kim with a yellow banana. Jay holds a book. Jay says, "I want a ball." Kim has no ball.
look.prompt: What could Kim do to get the book?

check.q: Why can't Kim trade with Jay?
choices: Jay does not want a banana
check.why: Jay wants a ball. He does not want what Kim has.

check.q: What is barter?
check.why: Barter means trading things, with no money.

check.q: Why was trading slow long ago?
choices: It was hard to find the right person
check.why: You had to find someone who wanted what you had.

lessons.title: Why We Use Money
lessons.mainIdea: Money is something everyone agrees to take in a trade.
reading: *Money* is something people agree to take when they trade. Coins and bills are money.
Kim sells her banana for money. Then she uses the money to buy the book. She does not need Jay to want a banana.
Money makes trading easy. Everyone takes it. You can use it to buy many different things.

words.d: coins and bills that people agree to take when they buy and sell

look.title: Kim Uses Money
look.text: Kim sells her banana to Lee. Lee pays her coins. Kim walks to Jay. She pays Jay the coins for his book.
look.prompt: How did money help Kim get the book?

check.q: Why is money helpful?
check.why: Money works because people agree to take it.

check.q: Kim sells a banana, then buys a book. What did she use?
check.why: She sold for money and used it to buy.

check.q: Which is money?
check.why: Coins like a dime are money.

lessons.title: Prices Tell the Cost
lessons.mainIdea: A price tells how much money a thing costs.
reading: A *price* tells how much money you pay for something. Stores put prices on signs and tags.
Look at a store sign. A pencil costs 25 cents (an example). A notebook costs $1 (an example). The notebook costs more.
You read the price before you buy. It helps you know if you have enough money to pay.

words.d: how much money something costs

look.title: School Store Prices
look.cite: Made-up example prices for a class store
look.prompt: Which thing costs the most? Which costs the least?

check.q: What does a price tell you?
check.why: A price is how much money you pay.

check.q: A pencil is 25 cents. An eraser is 10 cents. Which costs more?
check.why: 25 cents is more than 10 cents.

check.q: Why look at a price before you buy?
choices: To know if you have enough money
check.why: The price tells if your money is enough.

lessons.title: Coins and What They Are Worth
lessons.mainIdea: Each coin is worth a set number of cents.
reading: A *coin* is round money made of metal. A penny is worth 1 cent. A nickel is 5 cents.
A dime is 10 cents. A quarter is 25 cents. A dime is small, but it is worth more than a nickel.
A dollar is 100 cents. Four quarters make one dollar. Ten dimes make one dollar too.

words.d: round metal money, like a penny, nickel, dime or quarter
a small part of a dollar; 100 cents make one dollar

look.title: What Each Coin Is Worth
look.cite: U.S. coin values, United States Mint
look.prompt: Which coin is worth the most? How many nickels make a dime?

check.q: How many cents is a dime?
check.why: A dime is worth 10 cents.

check.q: How many quarters make one dollar?
check.why: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100 cents, one dollar.

check.q: Which coin is worth more?
check.why: A dime is 10 cents. A nickel is 5. A penny is 1.

lessons.title: Paying and Getting Change
lessons.mainIdea: If you pay more than the price, you get change back.
reading: Sometimes you pay more than the price. The seller gives some money back. This is called *change*.
A cookie costs 75 cents (an example). You pay with one dollar. One dollar is 100 cents. 100 take away 75 is 25. You get one quarter back.
Always count your change with care. It should match what you paid, take away the price.

words.d: money you get back when you pay more than the price

look.title: At the Bake Sale
look.text: A muffin costs 50 cents (an example). Rosa pays with one dollar bill. The seller opens the money box.
look.prompt: How much change should Rosa get?

check.q: A cookie costs 75 cents. You pay $1. What is your change?
A muffin costs 50 cents. You pay $1. What is your change?
What is change?
check.why: Change is money back when you pay more than the price.

lessons.title: Earning Money by Working
lessons.mainIdea: People earn money by doing work.
reading: Where does money come from? Most people *earn* it. They do work. They get paid money.
A baker makes bread. A bus driver drives the bus. Each one is paid for the work.
Kids can earn too. Pia helps rake leaves. Her neighbor pays her $2 (an example). Pia earned $2.

words.d: to get money for doing work

look.title: Pia Rakes Leaves
look.text: Pia rakes a big pile of red leaves. Her neighbor smiles. He gives Pia two dollar bills (an example).
look.prompt: How did Pia get her money?

check.q: How do most people get money?
check.why: Most people earn money by working.

check.q: Pia rakes leaves and gets $2. What did she do?
check.why: She did work and got paid. She earned it.

check.q: Who earns money for work?
check.why: A bus driver is paid for driving.

review.why: Everyone takes money, so trading is easy.

review.q: How many cents is a quarter?
A pencil costs 25 cents. You pay 50 cents. What is your change?
What does a price tell you?
review.why: A price is how much money it costs.

chapters.title: Save, Spend or Share
chapters.bigQuestion: How can I use my money to get what matters to me?

story.title: Deshawn's Three Jars
story.kicker: Deshawn has three jars, and one week the spend jar is empty.
paragraphs: Deshawn has three jars on his shelf. One says SAVE. One says SPEND. One says SHARE. Each week he helps feed the dog. He earns $3 (an example). He puts $1 in each jar.
One Saturday, Deshawn saw a toy ball at the store. He ran to his spend jar. It was empty! He had spent it all on snacks last week.
He looked at his save jar. It had $4 in it. He was saving for a kite. Should he take money from it? He thought hard. He left the save jar alone.
Two weeks later, the save jar had $6. That was enough for the kite (an example price). Deshawn flew it at the park. Waiting felt good.
story.think: Why did Deshawn leave his save jar alone?

lessons.title: What Saving Means
lessons.mainIdea: Saving means keeping money now to use later.
reading: To *save* means to keep money for later. You do not spend it today. You wait for later.
You might put coins in a piggy bank. Each week, you add a little more. The pile grows.
Saving helps you buy bigger things. You wait, and your money adds up over time. Hooray!

words.d: to keep money now so you can use it later

look.title: The Piggy Bank
look.text: Look at a pink piggy bank on a shelf. Each Friday, Nora drops in one quarter. Clink! It gets heavier.
look.prompt: What happens to Nora's money over many weeks?

check.q: What does save mean?
check.why: Saving is keeping money to use later.

check.q: Nora adds a coin each week. What happens?
check.why: Adding each week makes the pile grow.

check.q: Why should you save?
check.why: Saving lets money add up for a big thing.

lessons.title: Making a Saving Plan
lessons.mainIdea: A plan tells you how many weeks to save.
reading: A *goal* is something you want to get. A plan helps you reach it, one step at a time.
Tia wants a book. It costs $5 (an example). She gets $1 a week. After 1 week she has $1. After 5 weeks she has $5.
So Tia needs five weeks. Counting the weeks helps her wait. She knows when she will have enough.

words.d: something you want and work toward

look.title: Tia Saves for a Book
look.prompt: In which week does Tia have $5 for the book?

check.q: Tia saves $1 a week for a $5 book. How many weeks?
check.why: $1 each week for 5 weeks is $5.

check.q: What is a goal?
choices: Something you want and work toward
check.why: A goal is what you are working to get.

check.q: Tia has saved $3. The book is $5. How much more does she need?
check.why: 5 - 3 = 2 dollars.

lessons.title: Spending Money
lessons.mainIdea: Spending means using money to buy something.
reading: To *spend* means to use money to buy something. You give money. You get a thing.
Sam has $2 (an example). A snack costs $2 (an example). If he buys it, his money is gone.
Spending is fine. But once money is spent, you cannot spend it again. Think first.

words.d: to use money to buy something

look.title: Sam at the Store
look.text: Sam holds two dollar bills. He sees a snack for $2 and a small car for $2 (example prices). He can buy just one.
look.prompt: Which would you pick? What do you give up?

check.q: What does spend mean?
check.why: Spending is using money to buy.

check.q: Sam has $2 and buys a $2 snack. How much is left?
check.why: 2 - 2 = 0 dollars.

check.q: Sam can buy a snack or a car, not both. Why?
choices: He only has enough for one
check.why: His $2 buys just one $2 thing.

lessons.title: Save or Spend? You Choose
lessons.mainIdea: When you spend now, you give up saving for later.
reading: You cannot spend and save the same dollar. You must make a *choice*. Which one will you pick?
Deshawn spent his money on snacks. Then he had none for the ball. He gave up the ball to get the snacks.
Before you spend, ask: Is this a need or a want? Is there something I want more later?

words.d: picking one thing when you cannot have everything

look.title: Now or Later?
look.text: Ella has $1 (an example). A sticker costs $1 now. She is saving for a $5 puzzle (an example).
look.prompt: If Ella buys the sticker, what happens to her puzzle plan?

check.q: Ella spends $1 on a sticker. What does she give up?
check.why: That dollar can no longer go to the puzzle.

check.q: Can you spend and save the same dollar?
check.why: Once you spend a dollar, it is gone.

check.q: What is a good question before you spend?
choices: Is this a need or a want?
check.why: Asking need or want helps you choose.

lessons.title: Sharing to Help Others
lessons.mainIdea: Sharing means giving some money to help others.
reading: To *share* means to give some of what you have. Some people give money to help others.
Deshawn puts $1 in his share jar each week (an example). After a while, he gives it to the animal shelter. It helps buy food for pets.
Sharing is a choice too. Many families like to save, spend and share their money.

words.d: to give some of what you have to help others

look.title: The Share Jar
look.text: Look at Deshawn's share jar. It has four dollar bills inside (an example). The animal shelter needs dog food.
look.prompt: How could Deshawn's share jar help?

check.q: What does share mean?
check.why: Sharing is giving to help.

check.q: Deshawn puts $1 a week in his share jar. After 4 weeks, how much?
check.why: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 dollars.

check.q: What are the three jars?
check.why: The three jars are save, spend and share.

lessons.title: A Bank Keeps Money Safe
lessons.mainIdea: A bank is a safe place to keep money.
reading: A *bank* is a business that keeps money safe. People put money in a bank account.
At home, a jar can get lost or broken. At a bank, the money is kept safe and written down.
You can take your money out later when you need it. It is still all your own money.

words.d: a business that keeps people's money safe

look.title: Jar or Bank?
look.text: Picture Leo's jar with $20 in it (an example). His little brother knocks it off the table. Crash!
look.prompt: Why might Leo keep his money in a bank instead?

check.q: What does a bank do?
check.why: A bank keeps people's money safe.

check.q: Can you get your money back from a bank?
choices: Only the bank can use it
check.why: You can take your money out later.

check.q: Why is a bank safer than a jar?
choices: A jar can get lost or broken
check.why: Money at a bank is kept safe.

review.why: Saving is keeping money for later.

review.q: A game costs $4 (an example). You save $1 a week. How many weeks?

review.why: Spending is using money to buy.
Sharing is giving to help others.

review.q: Where can you keep money safe?
You spend your dollar on candy. What do you give up?
review.why: You cannot spend and save the same dollar.
